analysis.one_liner: Ends bulk government collection of Americans' phone records and adds oversight and transparency to secret surveillance courts.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 303-121 with 152 cosponsors from both parties, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2013 revelations about the NSA's bulk collection of Americans' phone call records, this bill would have required the government to name a specific person, account, or device before demanding records under the Patriot Act's business-records power. It would have barred bulk collection of call records, phone-line records, and national security letter demands; let judges appoint a privacy-minded adviser in secret surveillance court cases; required declassification of major court decisions; and let phone and internet companies tell the public how many government orders they receive. The House passed it by a wide bipartisan margin, but the Senate never took a vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday phone and internet users, whose call records had been collected in bulk without being tied to any specific suspicion. The bill would have required the government to name a specific person, account, or device as the basis for every records demand, capped daily call-record production at 180 days and two 'hops' from a suspect, and required destruction of collected records within five years. It also would have benefited the companies that hold that data, by letting them publish how many surveillance orders they receive and shielding them from lawsuits for complying.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits FISA courts from authorizing collection of any business records without a 'specific selection term' — a term identifying a particular person, entity, account, address, or device — ending bulk collection of Americans' records.

Caps court-ordered daily production of call detail records at 180 days, limits the government to two 'hops' of call records from a suspect, and requires prompt destruction of collected records that are not foreign intelligence information.

Requires the secret FISA court to appoint a privacy-and-civil-liberties expert to argue against the government in cases presenting novel legal questions, and requires declassification of significant FISA court decisions to the greatest extent practicable.

Lets phone and internet companies publicly report, in agreed number bands, how many national security orders and letters they received each half-year, and expands government reporting on FISA orders and national security letters.
Extends liability protections to companies providing technical assistance and requires the government to compensate them for their expenses in complying with call-detail-record orders.

analysis.who_pays: The National Security Agency and FBI lose their bulk-collection tool and take on new reporting, minimization, and audit requirements. Telecommunications and internet companies keep complying with government demands, now targeted rather than bulk, and are compensated for the expense. National-security officials also argue that targeted, case-by-case collection is slower and less capable than collecting everything at once.
analysis.who_pays_short: Intelligence agencies, and firms serving surveillance orders

drawbacks.text: The House-passed version was weaker than the bill originally introduced: the introduced version had included an independent 'Special Advocate' to argue privacy cases, a prohibition on searching Americans' communications already in government databases, minimization rules barring retention of wholly domestic communications, and a provision sunsetting certain national-security-letter authorities back to their pre-9/11 scope; the House-passed version replaced the Special Advocate with a more limited court-appointed amicus adviser and dropped the rest of those provisions.

The bill extends the sunset dates of the Patriot Act's business-records power, roving surveillance, and the 'lone wolf' provision from June 1, 2015 to December 31, 2017, keeping those authorities on the books for another two and a half years.

It still authorizes daily production of call detail records for counterterrorism investigations, permits two additional 'hops' of call records from any suspect, and lets the Attorney General order emergency production of records for up to seven days without a court order.

The emergency production authority bars use of information in court only if the follow-up court application is denied or the production is otherwise terminated without an order; information from productions that are approved retroactively can be used, and national-security officials argued bulk records were a valuable investigative tool the reform would cost them.
Company transparency reports are only allowed in coarse number bands, and new first-time disclosures can be delayed by up to two years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the core gain was real: ending bulk collection of their call records and opening the secret surveillance court to an independent privacy voice and public declassification. But the House-passed version was a negotiated compromise — softer than the bill its author introduced — and it came packaged with a two-and-a-half-year extension of the very Patriot Act powers it was reforming. Civil libertarians who wanted deeper cuts to surveillance authority saw it as too modest, while intelligence officials saw it as too restrictive; that squeeze from both sides is part of why it stalled in the Senate.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 303-121, but after the Senate received it in June 2014 it was referred to committee and only hearings were ever held — no Senate vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on October 29, 2013 and attracted 152 cosponsors, 80 Democrats and 72 Republicans.
The House Judiciary Committee reported it on a unanimous 32-0 vote, and the House passed it on May 22, 2014, 303-121 — Republicans voting 179-51 for it and Democrats 124-70 for it.

The Senate received the House-passed bill on June 2, 2014 and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; the Select Committee on Intelligence held hearings on June 5, 2014, but the Senate never brought the bill to a vote.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still stuck in Senate committee, so every provision died with the Congress.
The USA FREEDOM Act concept resurfaced in the next Congress and was enacted in June 2015 with substantially similar restrictions on bulk collection.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the near term, the surveillance status quo: the bulk records program and the Patriot Act provisions it rested on continued into the next Congress unchanged, and the transparency and court-reform provisions never took effect. Reform advocates ultimately got a version of the same law in 2015, so the delay cost about a year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The surveillance status quo, for another year

for.what_they_did: Marked the bill up and reported it to the House, Judiciary on a 32-0 vote.

for.role: Providers subject to FISA orders and privacy advocates
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported the bill's transparency provisions and its end to bulk collection of their customers' records.

against.what_they_did: Voted against passage — some because it preserved too much surveillance authority, others because it restricted it.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines in the House — Republicans voted 179-51 for it and Democrats 124-70 for it — with opposition on both sides coming from members who thought it went either too far or not far enough.

industries.note: The bill keeps these companies as the channel through which surveillance orders are served, but gives them something they had sought after the 2013 disclosures: the right to publish how many government orders they receive (in agreed number bands), expanded liability protection, and government compensation for compliance costs. Their interest in transparency and reduced bulk demands runs alongside their customers' privacy interests.

The bill takes away the bulk-collection tool the agencies had used under Section 215 and adds audit, minimization, and reporting requirements, but it also extends the Patriot Act authorities it reforms from June 2015 to December 2017 and preserves targeted collection with two 'hops' and emergency production without a prior court order. Their preference for broad, quickly available collection runs against the public's interest in privacy limits.

National security letter demands for customer financial and credit information would have to be tied to a specific selection term, narrowing what the FBI can sweep in, though the institutions remain compulsory providers of the information.
